Market Outlook
12Escalation in the Middle East & Shipping Impacts
Key Route Disruptions
•Strait of Hormuz  – effectively avoided by many commercial vessels due to 
safety advisories and threat warnings.
•Red Sea – The Red Sea remains a strategic but volatile maritime corridor.
•RCL has no Own vessels in 
the area.
•A chartered vessel could be 
used for a shuttle within.
•Cargos will be discharged at 
Sohar, Oman , and will be 
trucked to the nearest safe port for further transportation.Cost Structures Changing  – higher insurance, bunker, and schedule 
penalties likely.
•Insurance – Insurance premiums for Gulf transits have risen sharply.
•Fuel – Higher fuel and operating costs from rerouting and extended 
voyages.
•Freight – Upward pressure on freight rates, insurance surcharges, concern 
of cargo shortage, and logistical costs for shippers.
Demand & Supply Linkages – energy price volatility adds a macro layer to 
shipping demand patterns.
Broader Trade & Export Sentiment
Exporters in countries, e.g., India, have highlighted potential shipment reroutes through the Cape of Good Hope , adding 15 –20 days to transit time for cargo 
bound to Europe and the U.S., increasing logistics costs and complexity.

Enhancing Middle East and Red Sea Connectivity
The introduction of the RCL China Redsea Direct (RCR) service offers a dedicated Far East –Red Sea route, facilitating improved market access to key Red Sea 
gateways such as Jordan and Egypt. Utilizing Jeddah as a strategic hub, this service enables broader connectivity to additional Red Sea destinations, including Sudan and Somaliland, through efficient hub linkages.
